title: Forty Years of The Legend of Zelda: A Scoping Review of Game Design, Computation, Culture, and Play
content: Over four decades, The Legend of Zelda has evolved from a landmark action-adventure series into a recurring object of research across game studies, computer science, musicology, cultural studies, psychology, education, and related fields. This article presents a scoping review and structured survey of Zelda-related research across the franchise’s 1986–2026 history, examining how the series has been studied as a designed system, cultural artifact, interactive narrative, audiovisual environment, player-community object, and computational testbed. Following a PRISMA-ScR-informed process with duplicate screening and full-text eligibility assessment, 93 studies were included in the final synthesis: 52 Core scholarly studies, 40 complementary scholarly/grey-literature studies, and one complementary critical/industry record. The literature is strongly recent and unevenly distributed: 65 included studies were published from 2020 onward, while 44 explicitly address either Ocarina of Time or Breath of the Wild. Narrative and worldbuilding constitute the largest thematic area, whereas technology remains comparatively underrepresented as a primary research topic. In contrast, Zelda dungeon structures have become established computational objects for procedural content generation, formal modeling, and mixed-initiative design research. A sensitivity analysis restricted to the 52-study Core scholarly corpus preserved the principal distributional patterns, indicating that the main mapping conclusions are not driven by complementary evidence. Across the reviewed traditions, a recurring pattern is the interaction among spatial design, player agency, audiovisual feedback, narrative, and increasingly interoperable game systems. The survey identifies gaps in longitudinal analysis, technical research, visual studies, localization, empirical player research, and computational models of modern three-dimensional Zelda environments, positioning the franchise as a distinctive longitudinal case for studying the relationships among game design, technology, culture, computation, and play.
